title: Opportunity across the Employee Life Cycle
before: Explore how information, preparation, support, and recognition shape opportunity for DSD staff across the employee life cycle.

turns.text: This discussion opens Opportunity across the Employee Life Cycle. It’s about how information, preparation, support, and recognition shape who gets to develop in their work at DSD, from entering a role through growing within it. The course begins with a familiar pattern. The same employees keep receiving a practice policy-learning assignment because they’ve done it before.

And others have never had a route to gain that experience. The course doesn’t assume anyone’s motives from that pattern. It asks a more useful question: which entry requirements are genuinely necessary, and which describe the very capability the opportunity is meant to develop? If the requirement is the experience itself, the loop can keep repeating.

The course treats the life cycle as a connected path. Recruitment, selection, onboarding, assignments, development, recognition, advancement, and exit each involve different choices and conditions. A barrier at one stage can affect evidence used later. So rather than treating each decision as a complete explanation, we trace the possible connection between them.

Information is one of those conditions. Someone may hear informally about a project before the wider invitation goes out, and that gives them time to prepare. The course is clear that the relationship isn’t automatically wrong. The question is whether consequential information and a usable way to express interest become available to others through the actual process.

It also separates familiarity from task evidence. Confidence in a colleague we know well doesn’t by itself show the capability a task requires. Criteria should be explainable and relevant to the task, and a shared communication style or background shouldn’t quietly stand in for evidence. A visible invitation can still be unusable if the description, support, or practical burden gets in the way.

One boundary matters here. A learning label doesn’t change actual requirements for duties, classification, compensation, selection, or promotion. Those stay with the appropriate employment responsibilities and applicable agreements. Within that, the course asks about support. An assignment can carry a promising title while leaving the person without materials, feedback, or time. You’ll practice with a situation like that.

Recognition carries evidence forward too. Describing the actual contribution, including others’ work, matters because visibility isn’t the same as authorship. The course also connects internal opportunity to service knowledge. If the same staff always receive community or service-review assignments, understanding of later policy questions can become concentrated in a narrow circle.

That connects to identity. You’ll look at a project where one employee is repeatedly asked to represent a whole community because of their identity, without anyone discussing their interests or relevant expertise. The course is clear that community knowledge is not an identity duty. Culture briefs can prepare questions, but they don’t establish whose interests or knowledge fit an assignment.

There’s also attention to people who didn’t apply. A final participant list can’t tell us who heard about an opportunity, considered it, or declined. People have different goals, and some meet practical barriers. The course asks us to examine the route without penalizing a decision not to participate or demanding a personal explanation.

In the rewrite activity, you’ll name a task’s necessary entry capability and a capability the opportunity aims to develop, and explain the difference in your own words. The course is careful about privacy, with no private relationship maps or personal assessments. And it makes clear the aim isn’t to police friendships, but to keep familiarity from becoming an unstated prerequisite.

As you work through it, think of an opportunity in your own work: an assignment, a project, a training, or a stretch role. How did people find out about it, and what preparation did it assume? Bring that example along. The practice will help you examine the path before and after selection without ranking people or promising a career outcome.

guidance.title: Tracing one opportunity back
guidance.text: Pick a recent selection for an assignment or project and work backward. Who knew it was coming, and when? What earlier experience did it ask for, and how did people get that experience? Each step may have been reasonable on its own. Looking at the steps together can show where a route was open to some colleagues and never usable for others.

guidance.title: Making the route clearer
guidance.text: Think about a work relationship that has helped you learn about opportunities. That support has real value. Now consider a colleague who may not have the same connection. What essential information or route to express interest could you help make clearer for them, within your role, without removing a genuine requirement or assuming what their goals are?
